item.title: A Diminished Justice Dept. Braces for Fresh Fights After Midterm Loss
item.description:
A top Justice Department official delivered a gung-ho message to Trump-appointed federal prosecutors around the country on Monday, as they reckoned with the Republican drubbing in the midterm elections: We are now a wartime department, he declared.

The official, Aakash Singh, the principal associate deputy attorney general, exhorted dozens of U.S. attorneys during a teleconference call to step up their pressure on emboldened local officials in Democratic-controlled localities, like Houston, to cooperate with federal immigration enforcement, according to three people briefed on the exchange.

But it is hard to double down when you are running low on chips.

The department, which has already seen the exodus of hundreds of career officials who were forced out or left because they disagreed with President Trump’s priorities, faces a daunting new staffing dilemma spurred by the election.

Many career officials who hung on until now, including some who broadly support the department’s current mission, are eyeing the exits to avoid two grim years of partisan combat. They are joined by a second, higher-profile group: senior department officials who have submitted resignations, some after a discreet shove, in a leadership reshuffle over the past week.

Among the departures: Brett Shumate, the head of the department’s civil division; Harmeet Dhillon, the chief of the civil rights unit; and Jason Reding Quiñones, the U.S. attorney in Miami who oversaw a sprawling inquiry examining the various investigations into Mr. Trump. T. Elliot Gaiser, the head of the Justice Department’s Office of Legal Counsel, and Jesus A. Osete, a Dhillon aide, have been nominated for federal judgeships.

Patrick Davis, the former head of the department’s legislative affairs office, left before the election — averting the possibility that he would have to confront a torrent of congressional action.

The upheaval is hardly a surprise. Democrats will soon have the power to try to constrain Mr. Trump’s authority to directly control the department for the first time since his victory two years ago. Representative Robert Garcia, the California Democrat who is the top member of the House Oversight Committee, has taunted administration officials to “lawyer up,” promising wide-ranging investigations into Mr. Trump and those in his orbit.

Former officials now at private law firms said they were receiving calls from officials on the inside reporting that morale, already sagging, had gotten much worse since Election Day.

Yet not everyone is quite so glum.

“The departure of some of these lawyers from D.O.J. will no doubt be met with cheers from career prosecutors,” said Barbara McQuade, the U.S. attorney for the Eastern District of Michigan during the Obama administration.

“This has the feel of rats fleeing the sinking ship,” added Ms. McQuade, now a professor at the University of Michigan Law School.

Attorney General Todd Blanche has made clear that he intends to use the Justice Department to fight off any attempts by Congress to investigate administration officials, including Stephen Miller, the new White House chief of staff.

“I’ll tell you what,” Mr. Blanche said in a TV interview in recent days. “Stephen Miller has a lawyer. It’s me. It’s me and the entire Department of Justice.”

In another interview, Mr. Blanche adopted a less confrontational posture and said he would obey the law and comply with any reasonable congressional inquiry, although he did not say how he would make such a determination.

Kiersten Pels, a department spokeswoman, said Mr. Singh’s comments to the U.S. attorneys were not a declaration of political war but rather a reiteration of his determination to pursue law-and-order policies in the face of unwarranted local opposition.

“The ‘wartime’ reference had everything to do with public safety,” she said in an email. “In several districts, newly elected state and local leaders are no longer interested in partnering with federal law enforcement to keep their communities safe.”

The tone of defiance from Mr. Blanche and Mr. Singh is not shared by many of their younger subordinates, who are considering a near-term future that promises more provocations from Mr. Miller, perpetual congressional investigations and the possibility that their association with the Trump administration will crimp their future hiring prospects, according to former officials.

The department’s work force has, as a whole, been stressed by mass departures and the pressure to execute on Mr. Trump’s demands and Mr. Miller’s drive to increase the department’s criminal prosecutions of immigrants.

One example: The acting head of the U.S. attorney’s office for the Western District of Washington acknowledged to a federal judge in recent weeks that he did not have the staffing capacity to represent the government in all the cases in which immigrants legally challenged their detention.

Among the most striking features of the Justice Department under Mr. Blanche is its shrinking, centralized and overworked leadership core.

One former prosecutor who left earlier this year offered a mordant assessment: If the burger chain is called Five Guys, he joked, the Justice Department should be called Four Guys, to reflect its tiny leadership cadre — Mr. Blanche; his top deputy, Trent McCotter; Stanley Woodward Jr., the associate attorney general; and Mr. Singh, a veteran prosecutor responsible for an ever-expanding portfolio of criminal investigations.

Mr. Blanche’s three deputies have run themselves ragged in recent weeks, current officials said, to cope with the workload involving investigations into Mr. Trump’s perceived enemies, litigation over the president’s vanity construction projects and 11th-hour election cases in California and Alaska.

In many instances, they have been forced to personally oversee and sign complex legal filings that would have typically been handled by their subordinates, including the unsuccessful effort to preemptively block certification of the Senate race in Alaska if the Democratic candidate won by a narrow margin.

Ms. Dhillon, whose division had nominal jurisdiction in the matter, was notably absent from the lawsuit. She left soon after.

Mr. Shumate, for his part, has declined to sign on to unspecified litigation over the past several months, souring his relationship with the department’s leadership and some White House officials, according to a person with knowledge of the situation.

(Ms. Dhillon has declined to comment, and Mr. Shumate did not respond to a request for comment.)

It remains to be seen whether the recent shake-up was the product of the political tumult or part of a plan by Mr. Blanche to purge his leadership ranks of officials the White House saw as insufficiently capable of getting the job done — or a combination of both.

Thus far, only Ms. Dhillon has been replaced by an interim appointment.

Mr. Reding Quiñones, who had overseen a centerpiece of Mr. Trump’s retribution campaign, the so-called grand conspiracy inquiry of Obama-era officials, probably would have been ejected even if Republicans had fared better, people familiar with the situation said.

Yet his departure, along with those of others, removes a buffer for an attorney general bombarded with demands, many of them nearly impossible to fulfill, from an impatient White House. And Mr. Blanche will have to contend with the likelihood that many of these successors are unlikely to be confirmed by a Democratic-controlled Senate.

Mr. Blanche and his team will continue to confront the reality that cost his predecessor, Pam Bondi, her job — Mr. Trump’s insistence that he pursue investigations against political adversaries, often despite a lack of evidence and a questionable basis in the law.

Regardless of Mr. Trump’s calls, his revenge campaign has so far been largely unsuccessful. None of his most prized targets are in prison, although they have had to suffer the financial and reputational costs of investigation.

What the White House mostly has to show for these efforts is a remarkable string of losses in court. They include the increasing willingness of grand juries to reject indictments they see as specious, an occurrence that was once very rare, and a growing number of rebukes from judges appointed by both Republican and Democratic presidents.

Their actions have also created a small army of disgruntled department veterans, fired or driven from federal service, and seeking an arena to tell their own stories.

Suddenly, the voters have given them one.

These are likely to be the star witnesses in oversight hearings, revealing what they experienced firsthand to the general public — and seizing the narrative of grievance from Mr. Trump and those he chose to run the Justice Department.

Even as officials said that Mr. Singh was referring narrowly to the recalcitrance of local officials in blue states, there is little doubt that the administration will seek to project the image of an administration still capable of attacking. Before rejoining the administration, Mr. Miller founded a legal defense group that laid the groundwork for the department’s vengeance agenda.

On Monday, Will Scharf, the White House counsel, warned Mr. Garcia against congressional investigations by making the politically provocative but legally questionable claim that the lawmaker could face a criminal investigation for going over the line.

“We are monitoring the abusive and capricious threats that are now proliferating from Democrat legislators,” Mr. Scharf wrote.

The administration’s own frequent threats to Democrats over their public statements have thus far proved unpersuasive. An effort to indict six lawmakers last year, at Mr. Trump’s demand, was tossed out of court by a grand jury in the District of Columbia.

item.title: Soldier Shouts at Hegseth’s Group to Show ‘Respect’ at Tomb of the Unknowns
item.description:
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth was scolded on Wednesday at the Tomb of the Unknowns by an Army sentinel after laughter broke out among a group that accompanied him.

Mr. Hegseth, his wife and some advisers had been posing for pictures and chatting in front of the tomb, also called the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier, a solemn memorial at Arlington National Cemetery for military members who were killed in battle and remain unidentified.

Video recorded by reporters showed the sentinel guarding the tomb turning to face Mr. Hegseth’s group shortly after audible laughter from a woman among them.

“All visitors will maintain an atmosphere of silence and respect at all times,” the sentinel shouted toward Mr. Hegseth and others as they were leaving.

The rules for ceremonies at the cemetery prohibit visitors from yelling or making any other “boisterous” or “unreasonably loud” noise.

The defense secretary had been attending the annual Veterans Day wreath-laying ceremony at the cemetery alongside President Trump.

Sean Parnell, the Pentagon’s chief spokesman, said in a statement that the sentinels’ reaction was appropriate.

“The Secretary and the entire Department have always honored — and will always honor — the sacrifices our military men and women have made to keep America safe,” Mr. Parnell said. “While commemorating this solemn day, a soldier correctly and respectfully reminded everyone to maintain decorum.”

Guarding the tomb is a coveted position for an elite military unit, the 3rd U.S. Infantry Regiment, that stands watch there 24 hours a day. The tradition of standing continuously over the tomb dates back nearly nine decades.

The regiment, also known as “The Old Guard,” directed questions to Mr. Parnell.

With Mr. Hegseth on Wednesday were his wife, Jennifer Hegseth, and three advisers, Ricky Buria, Tami Radabaugh and Patrick Weaver.

It is not the first controversy related to decorum involving the president and his staff at the cemetery.

In 2024 a confrontation occurred between Mr. Trump’s campaign team and a cemetery official for taking photos and videos in a section of the burial reserved for American troops killed in recent wars. A statement from the cemetery at the time said that federal law prohibits political campaigning and related activities within Army cemeteries.

Mr. Trump had attended a wreath-laying ceremony for 13 American troops killed in a suicide bombing during the U.S. withdrawal from Afghanistan. Footage of Mr. Trump at the ceremony later appeared in a TikTok video released by his campaign.

And in 2017 during his first term, Mr. Trump visited the military grave of the son of John F. Kelly, a retired Marine general, and said, “I don’t get it. What was in it for them?”

Mr. Hegseth is a combat veteran who served in the Army National Guard. The defense secretary faced an impeachment bid in Congress on Tuesday that was ultimately shelved by House Republicans. Pressure has mounted on the defense secretary since last week’s midterm electoral outcome, which was driven in part by deep frustrations with the Iran war.

But Mr. Hegseth has continued to enjoy the support of Mr. Trump.

Shortly after the ceremony on Wednesday, Mr. Hegseth posted on social media a picture at the site of the ceremony with his wife.

“Happy Veterans Day — to our best Americans,” he wrote, adding, “Thank God for our warriors, past and present.”

Eric Schmitt contributed reporting.

item.title: Scott Colom, a Democrat, Wins Mississippi Senate Seat in Historic Upset
item.description:
The last Black man to represent Mississippi in the Senate was born into slavery and left office in 1881.

Nearly a century and a half later, Scott Colom, a Democrat, defeated Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith, Republican of Mississippi, according to The Associated Press, delivering a remarkable upset on Wednesday and becoming the first Black person to be elected to the Senate in his state since the Reconstruction era.

Mr. Colom’s victory, which came by a slim margin after more than a week of ballot tallying following the Nov. 3 election, puts an exclamation point on the sweeping Democratic victories across the country during this year’s midterms. For Republicans, the outcome was a jarring rebuke in a reliably conservative stronghold.

“God didn’t want us to get it the easy way,” Mr. Colom told the crowd gathered outside the historic chapel at Tougaloo College, a Black college that served as a haven for civil rights organizers. “He wanted us to get it the Mississippi way.”

Hours before he took the stage, Ms. Hyde-Smith conceded in a video posted to social media. “While this is not the outcome we worked for or hoped for, I respect the decision of Mississippi voters,” she said in the video. Ms. Hyde-Smith congratulated Mr. Colom and said her campaign “worked tirelessly to ensure every legally cast vote was counted, and that the people of Mississippi received a fair and transparent election.”

Mr. Colom’s victory was powered by a diverse coalition that included Black voters angered by policies that targeted their communities and their voting power; white voters frustrated with high prices and the Trump administration’s agenda; and some Republicans dissatisfied by Ms. Hyde-Smith’s loyalty to the president and his policies.

For much of this year, Ms. Hyde-Smith had been heavily favored to defeat Mr. Colom, a district attorney, and win a second term. President Trump carried Mississippi by 23 percentage points in 2024, and Republicans have long dominated statewide elections.

But the race appeared to tighten toward the end. Mr. Colom, who barreled across the state to homecoming celebrations, city halls and college campuses, worked to introduce himself and capitalize on frustration with Mr. Trump and his Republican allies.

The contest attracted national attention in its final stretch. Mr. Trump campaigned for Ms. Hyde-Smith in the state days before the election, while former President Bill Clinton and former Vice President Kamala Harris stumped for Mr. Colom.

As Democrats racked up win after win, taking back control of the House and Senate, the contest in Mississippi remained unsettled. Mr. Colom held a razor-thin lead as lawyers from both parties scrutinized the counting of mail votes as well as affidavit ballots, which are similar to provisional ballots in other states, cast by voters who were listed as inactive or did not bring proper identification.

As the cohort of newly elected senators headed to Washington for orientation, Mr. Colom waited in Mississippi for the results. It was fitting, he said, to spend time in the state as his supporters grew hopeful that he would emerge the winner.

“I had the courage to believe in Mississippi,” Mr. Colom said at the Tougaloo College chapel, where Fannie Lou Hamer and Medgar Evers once spoke. Before his speech, his supporters danced and embraced. One of them declared, “Thank the Lord, we did it.”

Mike Hurst, the chairman of the Mississippi Republican Party, said, “Scott Colom ran a good campaign here in Mississippi, and I congratulate him on his victory.”

He continued: “While elections may determine who holds public office, they do not define who we are as a people nor diminish the principles we hold dear. Tomorrow, the sun will rise over the same Mississippi we loved yesterday.”

During the campaign, Mr. Colom emphasized improving health care and lowering costs, among other issues. He did not often dwell on the historic implications of his candidacy, but took time on Wednesday to talk about the legacy he would now continue in Washington.

Mississippi was the first state to send a Black person to Congress, Hiram Revels, who joined the Senate in 1870. He was followed by Blanche Bruce in 1875, who was born in slavery in 1841. Mr. Bruce was replaced by a white former Confederate soldier who disavowed the ideals of racial equality and ushered in segregationist policies.

Mr. Colom will be sworn into office in January, 146 years after Mr. Bruce left office. And because both Mr. Revels and Mr. Bruce were chosen by state lawmakers, Mr. Colom is the first Black senator in the state’s history to be chosen by voters.

At a bar in downtown Jackson, Robert Morris, 37, sat on the patio and said the Senate election made history he never expected to witness as a lifelong resident of the Deep South. “I never thought I’d see a Black president, never thought I’d see a Black senator, especially a Black senator from Mississippi,” Morris said.

Mr. Colom’s victory came three years after Ms. Hyde-Smith denied him a chance at a seat on the federal judicial bench by blocking his nomination by President Joseph R. Biden Jr.

He announced his campaign to challenge her in September 2025, criticizing her reluctance to hold public town halls, as well as her unwavering support for Mr. Trump.

“Scott may have wanted to be a judge, but God saw fit for him to be someone who appoints judges,” said Jabari O. Edwards, a longtime friend of Mr. Colom.

His record as a prosecutor in northern Mississippi helped insulate him from attacks that he was too liberal for the state. Mr. Colom also hammered Ms. Hyde-Smith on her votes to cut health care and nutritional benefits, a potent message in one of the nation’s poorest states. And he created a viral campaign ad around her suggestion that voters contending with rising beef prices should “pick another protein,” encouraging Mississippi to “pick another senator instead.”

After the Supreme Court’s decision earlier this year to weaken the Voting Rights Act of 1965, he tapped into backlash among Black voters angered by attempts to dilute their voting power.

In the final weeks of the campaign, some Democratic-aligned groups injected money into the race, hoping to increase turnout. Even then, some were skeptical that a Democrat could break through in Mississippi.

“For the last couple days, I’ve been holding my breath,” said Ashley McKay, 38, who owns a Jackson restaurant and attended Mr. Colom’s victory speech. And on Wednesday, she said, she was feeling the “joy they talk about in the Bible — unspeakable joy.”

Michael Goldberg, politics reporter for Mississippi Today, contributed reporting from Jackson.

item.title: Democrats Face Backlash After Missing Hegseth Impeachment Vote
item.description:
Democrats, fresh off their sweeping victories in last week’s elections, faced bitter criticism and recriminations on Wednesday from within their own ranks after 11 of their members missed a vote on the impeachment of Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth.

The absences, which boosted Republicans’ successful effort to block the impeachment on Tuesday, cast a shadow over what was otherwise a triumphant week for Democrats that was supposed to be focused on savoring their electoral wins, welcoming new members and plotting out their agenda for when they take the helm of both chambers of Congress.

Instead, Representative Katherine Clark of Massachusetts, the No. 2 Democrat in charge of tracking votes among her members, began a closed-door party meeting on Wednesday morning scolding lawmakers who had been absent for the impeachment vote, as others chastised their colleagues in public.

“Show up and do your job,” Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed, Democrat of Michigan, said bluntly on CNN Tuesday evening.

Representative Sydney Kamlager-Dove, Democrat of California, appeared to be seething as she left the Capitol following the vote Tuesday night, telling the MeidasTouch Network that Democrats had squandered the opportunity to push the impeachment charges forward over Republican opposition. “People should have gotten their raggedy selves up these steps to vote,” she said.

Some senior Democrats said that more anger should be directed at Mr. Hegseth and the Republicans who banded together to save his job.

“People should have been here, right?” Representative Jim McGovern of Massachusetts, the top Democrat on the Rules Committee, said. “You know what people should be outraged by, is the fact that we have a secretary of war crimes who’s still there.”

Still, the episode raised questions about Democratic leaders’ hold on their caucus at a critical time. Representative Hakeem Jeffries of New York, the minority leader, said in the aftermath of the vote that he had yet to talk to members of his floor staff to find out what had happened. By Wednesday, he told reporters he had spoken to some of the absentees, many of whom had released statements explaining what had kept them from voting.

The absences muddled an opportunity for newly empowered Democrats to showcase their willingness to challenge the Trump administration even before taking power in January.

Republican leaders had worried privately that defections or absences by their members could allow the impeachment effort to succeed, particularly after many of them suffered embarrassing electoral defeats and had no political future to worry about.

Instead, they stayed united as Democratic no-shows helped Republicans prevail on a vote of 211 to 204, sending the impeachment charges to the Judiciary Committee and effectively killing them.

Eleven Democrats missed the vote, while seven Republicans did. Had all of those lawmakers voted along party lines, the G.O.P. effort to shelve the impeachment effort would still have succeeded.

Still, it was an embarrassing stumble that left many Democrats livid.

During her remarks at a closed-door caucus meeting Wednesday morning, Ms. Clark told Democratic colleagues she was disappointed in those who had missed the vote, according to a person present for the remarks who was granted anonymity to describe the private discussion.

Ms. Clark excused members kept away by serious illnesses or emergencies, but admonished those who had arrived late, regardless of the reason, telling them that the most fundamental responsibility of serving in Congress was to show up and vote.

The 11 Democrats who did not vote on the impeachment motion were Representatives Julia Brownley, Lou Correa and Nancy Pelosi, all of California; Laura Gillen of New York; Steven Horsford of Nevada; Jonathan L. Jackson of Illinois; Brittany Pettersen of Colorado; Melanie Stansbury of New Mexico; Haley Stevens of Michigan; Marilyn Strickland of Washington; and Frederica Wilson of Florida.

Their explanations for missing the vote varied.

Several cited traffic delays, including a handful who had attended a fund-raising event near the Capitol hosted by Ms. Clark. Ms. Stansbury, who posted on X Tuesday night saying she had missed the vote “due to a traffic incident,” apologized profusely in a video she posted on Wednesday in which she recounted having missed the vote because of “horrific” rush hour traffic and a police motorcade blocking the road.

Members of Ms. Pelosi’s staff said she was in California receiving a lifetime achievement award from a veterans group.

Mr. Correa said he was recovering from a medical procedure, while Mr. Horsford said a personal emergency had delayed his arrival.

Some, including Ms. Brownley, accused Republicans of closing the vote early to prevent Democrats from voting, though the roll call scheduled to last for 15 minutes lasted for 27 minutes. Ms. Pettersen, who last year returned to the Capitol with her newborn baby four weeks after giving birth to vote against the president’s domestic policy bill, said that she and others had been “denied the ability to vote” on the impeachment resolution. She accused Republican leaders of malfeasance.

Other Democrats suggested that no excuse was sufficient. Representative Pat Ryan, Democrat of New York, said he had undergone back surgery on Monday and “checked myself out of the hospital this morning to make sure I voted to impeach Hegseth.”

Democrats had previously scrambled in dramatic fashion to ensure they would have the votes to weigh in on impeachments. In 2024, Representative Al Green of Texas rushed from the hospital after undergoing emergency abdominal surgery and cast a decisive vote — still dressed in a hospital gown and socks — against impeaching Alejandro Mayorkas, President Joseph R. Biden Jr.’s homeland security secretary.

Asked what he thought about the Democratic absences on Tuesday given the elaborate lengths he had gone to cast his vote two years ago, Mr. Green grinned wryly.

“Believe me,” he said. “That came to mind when I saw that.”

Catie Edmondson contributed reporting.

item.title: 5 Things to Know About Democrat Scott Colom, Mississippi’s Next Senator
item.description:
In perhaps the most stunning upset of the midterm elections, Scott Colom, a Democrat from Mississippi, narrowly edged out Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith, a Republican, according to The Associated Press. The victory came after a vote count that extended more than a week after the Nov. 3 election.

Mr. Colom will become the first Black senator from Mississippi elected since Reconstruction, after Blanche K. Bruce, who was born into slavery, went to Washington more than 150 years ago.

Here are five things to know about Mr. Colom.

Mr. Colom, 43, is a district attorney from Columbus, Miss., a city of roughly 23,000 people near the border with Alabama. He won that office by unseating a nearly 30-year incumbent in 2015, and has been re-elected twice since then.

Mr. Colom’s mother was a judge, and his father, Wilbur Colom, is an attorney who served on Ronald Reagan’s transition team and ran as a Republican for state treasurer in 1987. Mr. Colom has two daughters with his wife and attends a Baptist church, according to his campaign website.

Mr. Colom is the first Black senator elected in more than 150 years from Mississippi, where Black residents make up 37 percent of the population — the highest proportion of any state. He is also the first Democrat to win a Senate race in the state since 1982, the year that John C. Stennis, a segregationist Democrat, ran for the last time.

Mr. Colom will take the seat once held by Hiram Revels, the nation’s first Black senator, who was elected in the Reconstruction era. The senator-elect did it by winning in a state that President Trump carried by nearly 23 points just two years ago.

Mr. Colom’s underdog bid attracted little national attention until October, when one of his campaign ads went viral. The video blasted Ms. Hyde-Smith for saying that voters “have so many proteins to choose from” in response to a local television anchor’s comment on the rising price of beef.

“Pick another protein?” a man asks in the ad as he flips a burger. “I’d rather pick another senator instead.”

The ad helped Mr. Colom inject energy into his campaign at a crucial moment. The main super PAC for Democratic Senate candidates spent $1.2 million on advertising for him shortly after the advertisement first ran, and added another $1 million later in the race.

Ms. Hyde-Smith was defeated by a man who, if not for her, would likely have been on the bench rather than on the campaign trail.

Three years ago, President Joseph R. Biden Jr. nominated Mr. Colom to a federal district court in Mississippi, and the state’s senior senator, Roger Wicker, a Republican, supported the move. But Ms. Hyde-Smith killed the nomination, objecting to Mr. Colom’s support for transgender rights and past spending on his behalf by a political action committee funded by George Soros, a billionaire donor to progressive causes.

Mr. Colom reached out to both Republicans and Democrats with promises that he would work across the aisle. He also spoke about high costs, his opposition to the Iran war, and his work prosecuting violent criminals.

On the campaign trail, he emphasized direct communication with voters. He held a series of “Where’s Cindy?” town halls to draw attention to his Republican opponent’s low profile in the state, parked a food truck outside small-town city halls and worked the line of attendees at a Trump rally in the final days before the election.

“I knew we could win,” Mr. Colom said at a news conference on Nov. 4. “I knew that there were voters out there who loved our state more than they loved a political party.”

Campbell Robertson and Emily Cochrane contributed reporting.

item.title: Colom’s win came down to a slow count of a few thousand ballots.
item.description:
Democrats who won seats in the Senate after the midterm elections posed for a group photo at the U.S. Capitol earlier this week. But Scott Colom was still in Mississippi, telling his supporters to hold on tight in a close Senate race that would be decided by a few thousand votes.

Mr. Colom, a Democrat, may be late to the party in Washington, but he finally made it. A decisive tranche of affidavit and absentee-by-mail ballots tallied on Wednesday pushed Mr. Colom to victory as the first Black senator elected by Mississippi since the Reconstruction era.

The counting took time. Tuesday was the last day that mail-in ballots postmarked on Election Day could arrive. By then, Mr. Colom held a narrow lead over the Republican incumbent, Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith, but it was not much larger than the roughly 2,500 absentee-by-mail ballots that still needed to be tallied.

There was also an unknown number of affidavit ballots left to be counted, and they were likely to play an outsized role in what had become an extremely close election. Those ballots had been cast provisionally by Mississippians who believed they were registered voters but who were not listed at their polling places.

Election officials had to check to see if those voters had been missed in poll books, or if they had later turned up at a local clerk’s office with proper identification to “cure” their ballots. The deadline to cure affidavit ballots was also on Tuesday.

The affidavit ballots are required to be manually processed by local officials, part of a slow count that had captured national attention since the Nov. 3 election.

The process to validate affidavit ballots had confused some younger voters, leading to efforts by organizers in recent days to get students on college campuses to check the status of their votes. Young voters were a key component of Mr. Colom’s coalition.

Unlike most states, Mississippi law does not allow for a recount in statewide races. But Republicans have closely monitored the count, with their lawyers writing to election commissioners that there should be an “immediate separation, secure custody, and preservation of all affidavit ballots.” Mr. Colom’s lawyers objected to that request in their own letter.

Mike Hurst, the chairman of the Mississippi Republican Party, had previously said lawyers supporting Ms. Hyde-Smith’s campaign “will be ready, if necessary, to avail ourselves of every legal option at our disposal, if there is evidence that the law has been violated.”

Emily Cochrane contributed reporting.

item.title: Long Before Scott Colom, There Were Hiram Revels and Blanche Bruce.
item.description:
With the race called in his favor on Wednesday, Scott Colom will become the third Black senator in Mississippi history, but the first in nearly 150 years. That legacy traces back to Feb. 25, 1870, when Hiram Revels walked into the chamber of the U.S. Senate to take his oath of office.

The month before, the Fifteenth Amendment had been ratified, giving Black men like Mr. Revels the right to vote in a nation that had been ravaged by the Civil War. Mr. Revels, a man born free in North Carolina who served as a Union Army chaplain in Mississippi, had been chosen by the Mississippi Legislature to be its first new senator after the Civil War.

Two days after the state was readmitted to the union, Mr. Revels became the first Black man ever seated in the Senate. He delivered his first speech on the Senate floor in opposition to an amendment that would stop Black people from holding office.

Black residents, he said, “ask but the rights which are theirs by God’s universal law.”

Mr. Revels was joined soon after in the Senate by Blanche K. Bruce, who was born into slavery in Virginia and fled to freedom at the start of the Civil War. He became the first Black man to serve a full term in the Senate.

Mr. Bruce served from 1875 to 1881, as Reconstruction in Mississippi was in its last, bloody days before white leaders ushered in the repressive Jim Crow era by stripping Black Mississippians of many of their rights. He raised alarms about violence against Black voters, but expressed confidence “in the endurance, capacity and destiny of my people.”

Two Black men — Mike Espy, who went on to serve as agriculture secretary during the Clinton administration, and Representative Bennie Thompson, who won re-election on Nov. 3 — have been elected by Mississippi to the House since Reconstruction.

The Senate had been more elusive. Mr. Revels’s seat would go on to be held by staunch segregationists including James K. Vardaman and James O. Eastland. In January, it will belong to Mr. Colom.

item.title: Colom’s Victory Pads Democrats’ Majority in the Senate
item.description:
Scott Colom’s victory in Mississippi adds to the Senate Democratic majority and gives the chamber a new Black voice from the rural South.

Mr. Colom’s win over the Republican incumbent, Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith, brings the Senate Democratic majority to at least 55 seats, with Alaska remaining to be decided as the Democrat Mary Peltola leads there over Senator Dan Sullivan, a Republican.

The larger margin of control gives Democrats more seats on committees, making it easer to overcome opposition there. It also puts the party closer to the 60-vote threshold to break a filibuster, meaning Democrats need to win fewer G.O.P. votes to avoid an impasse and advance bills, though they are still short of the supermajority needed to bypass Republicans entirely.

While Mr. Colom got some political help in his campaign from Senator Chuck Schumer, the New York Democrat and party leader, he has suggested he might not support Mr. Schumer’s bid to keep his top slot and become majority leader.

But his reasoning was different than that of other newcomers who have questioned whether Mr. Schumer is too old, too moderate and too aligned with the party establishment to continue at the top. Mr. Colom said his concern was that the two potential party leaders — Mr. Schumer and Representative Hakeem Jeffries, another establishment moderate from New York — both came from Brooklyn, suggesting that Democrats needed a wider range of viewpoints at the top.

A prosecutor, Mr. Colom could be expected to play a role on criminal justice issues. But he has also been focused on income inequality and access to health care as well as the struggles of smaller farmers in rural swaths of Mississippi.

item.title: A California Man Is on the Cusp of Election Victory. He Died Months Ago.
item.description:
Bruce Giudici spent years trying to win a seat on the board of supervisors in Calaveras County, Calif.

He seems to have succeeded now — though he died in August.

The most recent results, published by the Calaveras County authorities on Tuesday evening, show Mr. Giudici with 57 percent of the vote in this month’s election. That gives him a 497-vote lead over his opponent, Clyde Clapp.

Local officials believe there are about 500 ballots left to sort through countywide, but do not expect to issue another update until Friday. The current tally, though, suggests Mr. Giudici will almost certainly win.

Mr. Giudici’s campaign said he had been out knocking on doors when he fell on Aug. 30. Mr. Giudici, who was 68, died the next day.

The campaign pushed forward anyway.

The 47,000 residents in the county, southeast of Sacramento, have voted for Republican presidential candidates for decades, but candidates for supervisor run for four-year terms on a formally nonpartisan basis.

And those contests, like many local races across the country, often hinge more on mudslinging and grass-roots politicking than just about anything else.

Mr. Giudici’s supporters insisted that a vote for a dead candidate was better than the alternative, Mr. Clapp, whom they depicted as a man with a troubled past and a tendency to mislead would-be constituents.

“Bruce Giudici stood for fiscal responsibility, ethical leadership and putting people first,” his campaign wrote in a social media post last month. “Let’s honor his vision by voting BRUCE Nov. 3 and allowing the appointment process to find a similarly qualified District 5 resident to serve our community.”

Neither campaign responded to requests for comment on Wednesday.

Mr. Giudici had lived in the region for decades and had told voters that his professional life had prepared him for the board of supervisors, which is the county’s main governing body. He touted his years of nonprofit work, called himself a fiscal watchdog, and emphasized wildfire preparedness and road repairs, according to a voter information pamphlet.

Within days of Mr. Giudici’s death, his campaign began describing what, exactly, could transpire if the community elected a dead candidate.

The process, now virtually certain to happen, is rooted in state law: California’s incoming governor, Xavier Becerra, will appoint an interim supervisor to serve until the conclusion of another election that could happen in March 2028.

The circumstances in Calaveras County, which is perhaps most famous for its role in a Mark Twain short story, are not without precedent.

Voters across the country have, at least temporarily, opted for deceased candidates.

In 2000, for example, Missouri voters elected Mel Carnahan to a U.S. Senate seat weeks after he died in a plane crash; the governor later appointed Mr. Carnahan’s widow.

And two members of Congress — Hale Boggs of Louisiana and Nick Begich of Alaska — were re-elected even after a plane they were aboard disappeared before the 1972 election.

This year in Calaveras County, Mr. Giudici’s death was a stunning twist in a protracted political rivalry that began at least a decade ago.

In 2016, voters recalled the incumbent at the time and installed Mr. Clapp. Mr. Giudici finished third in the contest to replace the ousted supervisor.

Two years later, Mr. Clapp and Mr. Giudici met in a primary. Mr. Clapp advanced to the general election against another candidate but was defeated in his bid for a full term.

Ben Stopper, the current supervisor, ran for re-election but lost this year’s primary to Mr. Clapp and Mr. Giudici.

After Mr. Giudici died, Mr. Stopper told a local newspaper, The Union Democrat, that he would support him nevertheless.

“I’m still going to vote for him because he’s going to be on the ballot,” Mr. Stopper said. “He’s the best guy for the job, even in this situation, unfortunately.”

item.title: Hyde-Smith Concedes to Colom: ‘I Respect the Decision of Mississippi Voters’
item.description:
Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith, Republican of Mississippi, conceded to Scott Colom, a Democrat, in a video posted to social media on Wednesday evening.

“While this is not the outcome we worked for or hoped for, I respect the decision of Mississippi voters,” Ms. Hyde-Smith said in the video. “I want to congratulate Scott Colom and wish him well as he takes on the tremendous responsibility of representing our great state.”

Ms. Hyde-Smith said that her campaign “worked tirelessly to ensure every legally cast vote was counted, and that the people of Mississippi received a fair and transparent election.”

Mr. Colom defeated Ms. Hyde-Smith by a narrow margin, according to The Associated Press. He will become the first Black senator elected from Mississippi since Reconstruction.

Mr. Colom’s win means Democrats will hold at least 55 Senate seats at the start of the next Congress. The contest in Alaska, in which the Democrat Mary Peltola has a narrow lead, is the last remaining Senate race in which a winner has not been declared.

Ms. Hyde-Smith, the first woman to represent Mississippi in Congress, was first appointed to the Senate to fill a vacancy in April 2018. She had previously served as Mississippi’s commissioner of agriculture from 2012 to 2018.

The Republican senator also spent more than a decade in the Mississippi State Senate, starting as a conservative Democrat in 2000 and converting to the Republican Party in 2010.

item.title: Hyde-Smith Blocked Colom’s Path to the Bench. Now He’s Replacing Her.
item.description:
When it comes to lifetime judicial appointments, the Senate maintains a century-old tradition: The two home-state senators get virtual veto power, regardless of party.

Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith, Republican of Mississippi, used that authority in 2023 to single-handedly block Scott Colom, a district attorney, from consideration for a U.S. District Court vacancy in the state when the Biden administration nominated him.

Now, Mr. Colom, a Democrat, has defeated Ms. Hyde-Smith and will take her Senate seat in January.

Given the stability and authority of a lifetime appointment to the federal bench, Mr. Colom would not have sought the Senate seat had he been confirmed, he said. But he also stressed that his motivation for running was not a matter of retribution, but a deeper frustration with what he felt was a lack of attention to the state.

For Democrats and Mr. Colom’s allies, who were angered by Ms. Hyde-Smith’s rejection, there was some satisfaction in the election outcome on Wednesday.

“Scott may have wanted to be a judge, but God saw fit for him to be someone who appoints judges,” said Jabari O. Edwards, a longtime friend of Mr. Colom’s.

Mr. Colom, who defeated a three-decade incumbent to become district attorney, had labored to secure bipartisan support for the judicial nomination. He had the backing of Roger Wicker, the other Republican senator from the state; Representative Bennie Thompson, the powerful, long-serving Black Democrat; and two former Republican governors, Haley Barbour and Phil Bryant.

Ms. Hyde-Smith was unmoved.

“I simply cannot support his nomination to serve on the federal bench in Mississippi for a lifetime,” Ms. Hyde-Smith said in a statement in 2023.

Carl Hulse contributed reporting.

item.title: The Man at the Center of Scott Colom’s Protein Ad
item.description:
Russ Hudson was not supposed to be in Scott Colom’s protein ad.

Mr. Hudson, 35, had known the district attorney for about a decade before Mr. Colom became the Democratic candidate for Senate in Mississippi. But it was Mr. Hudson’s father who was initially cast in the campaign ad mocking a suggestion from Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith, the Republican incumbent, that Mississippi residents pick another type of protein to avoid rising beef prices.

When the elder Mr. Hudson balked at a script that would require him to utter profanity on camera, his son volunteered. In a short-sleeved button down shirt, he stood at a grill in the backyard of Mr. Colom’s parent’s house and tossed his head back to deliver a drawling, deadpan rebuke of Ms. Hyde-Smith.

“Shee-it,” Mr. Hudson says in the spot, rendering the off-color word with a distinct southern twang. “I’d rather pick another senator, instead.”

The lines, he said, felt natural. He left thinking maybe a couple thousand people would see it.

“I just did it like a Mississippian would,” Mr. Hudson said in an interview.

Now, Mr. Hudson, an Army veteran who served in Afghanistan, has found himself as the unlikely face of one of the most potent campaign advertisements of the 2026 midterm cycle. The ad, released in the final weeks of the election season, became a defining feature of Mr. Colom’s campaign and his surge to a stunning upset.

“I never expected it to do what it did,” Mr. Hudson said.

He even downloaded TikTok to keep up with all the commentary his friends were sending him about the ad. Someone made him a “pick another protein” shirt with his face on it, along with the other two women in the ad.

And he keeps fielding requests to, well, say it again.

“They make me throw my head back with it, too,” he said.

Mr. Hudson, who said he has been mocked for his Southern twang outside of the state, had not been heavily involved in politics. As a disabled veteran on a fixed income and father to an infant, he was drawn to Mr. Colom’s pledges to focus on high costs and protecting benefits for veterans, as well as the personal connection. The ad, he figured, was his contribution to the campaign.

“A lot of people don’t know much about Mississippi,” he said. “And look at us now. We’re worldwide.”

item.title: Judge Richard A. Posner Has Died. His Influence in Law Was Beyond Compare.
item.description:
Judge Richard A. Posner, whose protean intellect, relentless work ethic and startling candor made him a towering figure in the law, died on Tuesday in Chicago. He was 87.

His son Eric confirmed the death.

Judge Posner, who served from 1981 to 2017 on the United States Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit, in Chicago, wrote thousands of judicial opinions and more than 50 books on a vast array of topics, along with countless scholarly articles, essays, book reviews and blog posts.

He was, the journalist Gary Rosen wrote in The Wall Street Journal in 2002, “a one-man think tank.”

Judge Posner was the most-cited legal scholar in the second half of the 20th century, according to a 2000 study conducted by Fred R. Shapiro, beating the runner-up, Ronald Dworkin, by a factor of almost two.

In the casebooks that collect excerpts from judicial opinions and are the basis for much of legal education, Judge Posner’s work was featured for many years more often than that of any other judge. “The differential in terms of total influence on the casebooks between Posner and almost all the other judges is staggering,” the authors of a second study, Mitu Gulati and Veronica Sanchez, wrote in 2002.

When Professor Gulati and Stephen J. Choi updated the study this year, they found that little had changed. Judge Posner’s lead remained “astonishing,” they wrote.

Only two other American judges who did not serve on the Supreme Court had his stature: Judges Learned Hand and Henry J. Friendly, who both sat on the federal appeals court in New York.

Judge Posner’s admirers said he had no real competition in the annals of American jurisprudence. They regarded him as a superb writer, with a limpid, conversational style and a sure command of tone. He wrote with self-confidence and authority, qualities his critics said were not always entirely deserved. Most important, in a field that overvalues tradition and formalism, he was known as a brilliantly original iconoclast.

“Posner was the greatest and most skilled judge in American history,” Saul Levmore, a former dean of the University of Chicago Law School, wrote in an email. “Part of his influence was his willingness to think aloud, and in print, about what law may be trying to accomplish and how it might go about it.”

Judge Posner called his approach to judging pragmatic. His critics called it lawless. “I pay very little attention to legal rules, statutes, constitutional provisions,” Judge Posner said in a 2017 interview. “A case is just a dispute. The first thing you do is ask yourself — forget about the law — what is a sensible resolution of this dispute?”

How The Times decides who gets an obituary. There is no formula, scoring system or checklist in determining the news value of a life. We investigate, research and ask around before settling on our subjects. If you know of someone who might be a candidate for a Times obituary, please suggest it here.

He was among the leading figures in the movement to analyze legal problems using economics. In looking to social utility rather than abstract moral values like fairness or equality, he gained a reputation as a cold, calculating conservative.

He was just 33 when he published “Economic Analysis of Law,” a tour de force that helped establish the field, in 1972. He went on to write many books, among them ones about antitrust, law and literature, sex and reason, the impeachment of President Bill Clinton, the 2000 election recount and, after the Sept. 11 attacks, national security.

President Ronald Reagan appointed him to the Seventh Circuit in 1981, at the age of 42, and there was occasional talk of a Supreme Court nomination. Some of Judge Posner’s more extreme thought experiments — applying free-market principles to adoptions, or, as his critics would have it, “selling babies,” was the example most often cited — made other candidates more attractive.

In person, he was mild, a little distant and sometimes seemingly indifferent to ordinary social niceties. He was the first to acknowledge his own oddities. “I have exactly the same personality as my cat,” Judge Posner said in a memorable New Yorker profile. “I am cold, furtive, callous, snobbish, selfish and playful, but with a streak of cruelty.”

Judge Posner had no patience for the formalism of most legal reasoning and the jargon in most legal writing. Nor was he a fan of originalism, the mode of constitutional interpretation that seeks to unearth the original public meaning of the text of the Constitution. He was more interested in the practical consequences of his decisions.

Breaking with the norms of appellate adjudication, in which judges are expected to confine themselves to the record prepared in the trial court, Judge Posner conducted internet research and even experiments in his chambers.

For most of his judicial career, Judge Posner’s opinions generally reached conservative results, though often through routes at odds with the interpretive methods preferred by the increasingly influential conservative legal movement. He was interested in finding the sensible answer to the dispute before him and in announcing an efficient and workable legal principle to govern similar ones.

In later years, he drifted left, issuing opinions on voter ID laws, abortion, same-sex marriage and workplace discrimination based on sexual orientation that were markedly liberal.

His methodology remained largely unchanged. In 2013, for instance, he wrote an opinion blocking a Wisconsin law restricting abortions. Anticipating a 2016 Supreme Court decision, he wrote that courts must balance the supposed health benefits of abortion restrictions against the burdens they impose on access to abortion.

He was capable of changing his mind.

In 2007, he wrote a majority opinion upholding an Indiana voter ID law. In a 2013 book, “Reflections on Judging,” he confessed error. “I plead guilty,” he wrote, “to having written the majority opinion (affirmed by the Supreme Court) upholding Indiana’s requirement that prospective voters prove their identity with a photo ID — a type of law now widely regarded as a means of voter suppression rather than of fraud prevention.”

He elaborated in a 2014 dissent in a case on Wisconsin’s voter ID requirement, writing that such laws are “a mere fig leaf for efforts to disenfranchise voters likely to vote for the political party that does not control the state government.”

When he followed what he said were the Supreme Court’s commands, he sometimes appeared to do so grudgingly. In 2012, he wrote a majority opinion blocking an Illinois law that banned carrying guns in public, saying the result was required by a 2008 Supreme Court decision, District of Columbia v. Heller, which established an individual right for law-abiding citizens to keep guns in their homes for self-defense.

Judge Posner reviewed the empirical literature about the practical consequences for crime and safety of bans on carrying guns in public, and he found it inconclusive. “Anyway,” Judge Posner wrote, “the Supreme Court made clear in Heller that it wasn’t going to make the right to bear arms depend on casualty counts.”

He retired abruptly from the appeals court in 2017 after clashes with colleagues over what he said was the court’s mistreatment of litigants without lawyers.

Richard Allen Posner, an only child, was born in Manhattan on Jan. 11, 1939, to Max and Blanche (Hofrichter) Posner, both immigrants from Europe. They were, Judge Posner told a biographer, nonobservant Jews sympathetic to communism.

His father was a criminal lawyer but switched to a career in business, working as a mortgage lender for commercial properties, according to William Domnarski’s biography of Judge Posner.

The family moved to Scarsdale, N.Y., an affluent suburb of New York City, in 1948, and young Dick thrived in its public schools. He entered Yale University at 16, becoming an English major and producing a 321-page study of William Butler Yeats’s late poetry under the supervision of Cleanth Brooks, a prominent literary critic.

After receiving his Yale degree in 1959, he attended Harvard Law School, graduating first in his class in 1962 and serving as president of its law review. The experience made him a lifelong enemy of The Bluebook, an elaborate style manual that sets out detailed rules about how to cite judicial decisions, law review articles and the like.

“The vacuity and tendentiousness of so much legal reasoning are concealed by the awesome scrupulousness with which a set of intricate rules governing the form of citations is observed,” Judge Posner wrote in a review of The Bluebook’s 1986 edition.

After law school, he served as a U.S. Supreme Court law clerk to Justice William J. Brennan Jr. from 1962 to 1963. The justice’s liberal views matched those of the young clerk, and the two men forged a warm relationship. Justice Brennan was a master strategist, but he left the details to his clerks, and Mr. Posner drafted several important opinions, including N.A.A.C.P. v. Button, which protected the civil rights group’s membership lists.

From 1963 to 1965, Mr. Posner worked at the Federal Trade Commission, then was an assistant to the U.S. solicitor general, Thurgood Marshall, and argued six cases in the Supreme Court. He left that job after two years, later writing that the quality of the lawyers’ arguments did not seem to influence the justices’ decisions.

Mr. Posner spent a year on a presidential task force on communications policy before joining the legal academy, first at Stanford and then, starting in 1969, at the University of Chicago, where he would teach for many decades and play a prominent role in the founding and promotion of the law and economics movement.

While at the law school, he and two colleagues formed Lexecon, a successful consulting firm that advised companies on antitrust and regulatory matters. He left the firm in 1981, with his partners buying out his share, when Mr. Reagan nominated him to the Seventh Circuit. Judge Posner continued to teach at the law school after joining the appeals court.

On the bench, Judge Posner could be impatient and intimidating. In chambers, he was informal, telling his clerks to call him Dick. He wrote his own opinions, which is unusual for a modern federal appeals court judge.

In 1962, Judge Posner married Charlene Horn. In addition to his wife and son Eric, a law professor at the University of Chicago, he is survived by another son, Kenneth, an investment banker in New York; and four grandchildren.

Asked in 2017 by The New York Times about his many critics, Judge Posner said they fell into two camps.

Some, he said, simply have a different view of the proper role of the judge. “There is a very strong formalist tradition in the law,” he said, summarizing it as: “Judges are simply applying rules, and the rules come from somewhere else, like the Constitution, and the Constitution is sacred. And statutes, unless they’re unconstitutional, are sacred also.”

“A lot of the people who say that are sincere,” he said. “That’s their conception of law. That’s fine.”

He said he had less sympathy for the second camp. “There are others who are just, you know, reactionary beasts,” he said. “They’re reactionary beasts because they want to manipulate the statutes and the Constitution in their own way.”

item.title: Colom’s win fuels Democratic hopes for next year’s race for governor.
item.description:
The outcome of the Senate race in Mississippi is finally settled. But even before Scott Colom’s long-shot Democratic victory, voters, officials and politicians were already starting to look ahead to next year.

Mr. Colom’s win — driven by the diverse coalition he assembled of Black voters, white Democrats and disenchanted conservatives — has raised questions about how competitive next year’s race might be to replace Gov. Tate Reeves, a Republican who cannot seek another term under state law.

Two Democratic candidates have already announced plans to run, alongside an already crowded Republican field. Some Democrats have speculated that Brandon Presley, the second cousin of Elvis Presley who fell short in the 2023 race against Mr. Reeves, could run again and capitalize on the party’s enthusiasm in the aftermath of Mr. Colom’s win. (Asked directly on Friday, Mr. Presley did not answer.)

Shad White, the conservative state auditor, announced his campaign for governor this week, joining Attorney General Lynn Fitch and two other Republicans who had already announced.

The Senate race could reverberate in other ways.

Michael Watson, the Republican secretary of state who oversees elections, is running for lieutenant governor, but frustrations over the prolonged counting of ballots this year and the number of voters who found themselves listed as inactive could complicate his political ambitions.

The uptick in turnout from Black voters in the South, as well as the overwhelming Republican losses across the country this month, could also affect political calculations around whether to change Mississippi’s district lines in both the State Legislature and Congress.

After the Supreme Court ruling this year that weakened the Voting Rights Act of 1965, some Mississippi Republicans pushed for new lines to be drawn that would give them an advantage — and most likely undercut the power of Black voters in choosing state and federal representatives alike.

Before the election, lawmakers held a series of public hearings to debate the possibility of new district lines. Some organizers and voters said the prospect of mid-decade redistricting tied to the Voting Rights Act was yet another motivating factor for Black voters to go to the polls and support Democrats this year.

Campbell Robertson contributed reporting.

item.title: Mississippi Democrats built a coalition to elect a Black senator for the first time since Reconstruction.
item.description:
Scott Colom is set to become the first Black senator from Mississippi in more than 145 years thanks to an unparalleled coalition of hundreds of thousands of Black voters, white voters, enthusiastic college students, angry suburbanites and discontented small-town conservatives.

The circumstances behind Mr. Colom’s electoral performance may be a combination of hard work and luck, a skilled candidate running a sharp campaign at just the right time. But history hangs heavily over events in Mississippi, and the significance is profound.

Mr. Colom will take the seat once held by Hiram Revels, the nation’s first Black senator, who was elected in 1870, the middle of the Reconstruction era. The last Black senator from Mississippi, Blanche K. Bruce, served from 1875 to 1881, as Reconstruction was in its final days, raising alarms about the violence faced by Black voters but expressing his confidence “in the endurance, capacity and destiny of my people.”

This year’s huge Black turnout in the state was in part a reaction to efforts in Mississippi and elsewhere in the South to redraw district lines that would carve up majority-Black seats in Congress and in state legislatures.

Among Mr. Colom’s supporters, the prevailing sentiment is that a Black Democrat’s victory in the state was simply a matter of time. What seems so astounding to outsiders is seen by many here as a math problem that has finally been solved.

item.title: A viral ad and a Trump rally visit helped Colom compete in Mississippi.

item.title: San Antonio Fights Plan to Turn Warehouse Into ICE Detention Center
item.description:
With roughly seven weeks until a Democratic majority takes over Congress, San Antonio is using a lawsuit to stall the Trump administration’s plan to turn a warehouse into a detention center for 1,500 immigrants.

Representative Joaquin Castro, a Democrat who represents part of the city, hopes the party’s new majority in Congress can block the project for good when it takes power in January.

“We are just getting going now,” Mr. Castro said. “Those places, those warehouses, are not suited for people.”

The projects have faced resistance and legal defeats, and several have been scrapped.

In San Antonio, Mayor Gina Ortiz Jones and other officials have said they have been kept in the dark since February, when the government purchased the sprawling warehouse for $66 million.

The city sued last month to stop work there until the federal government studies its effects on its neighborhood, joining nearly a dozen other cities, states and nonprofit groups to challenge such plans in court.

“In their rush to convert warehouses into Amazon-like store-and-ship facilities for immigrants, defendants have trampled over federal law designed to protect the city and other stakeholders’ interests,” San Antonio’s lawsuit reads.

The city, like others that have sued, argues that the Department of Homeland Security, which oversees U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, has skipped legally required environmental reviews. The argument has already slowed the agency’s plans elsewhere: A federal judge in Maryland recently blocked a similar warehouse conversion on the same grounds. ICE has paused or dropped plans in at least five other states.

In San Antonio, the City Attorney’s Office said it was in talks with the Justice Department over a deal that would pause both the lawsuit and the work on the warehouse.

Ms. Jones said in a statement that she wants to cooperate with Democrats in Austin and Washington to resist ICE’s aggressive crackdown.

“I look forward to working with them on those approaches, which must include preventing the establishment of an ICE detention facility in San Antonio,” Ms. Jones said.

ICE did not respond to repeated requests for comment.

Under the Trump administration, immigration arrests have surged in San Antonio. The area, which is majority Latino, has an estimated 100,000 undocumented residents, city officials said.

At St. Margaret Mary Catholic Church, less than a 15-minute drive from the proposed detention center, fears have run rampant among the many immigrant parishioners, the Rev. Jimmy Drennan said. In the months before the midterm elections, many called him to ask for his help in locating missing loved ones, whom they presume have been taken by ICE.

The warehouse project makes the threat concrete, he said.

“They are going to fill it up with our children’s friends, colleagues, neighbors and the people who occupy our churches,” Father Drennan said.

Mayor Jones and Mr. Castro have said that the troubles at other such facilities in Texas are cautionary tales.

At the Dilley Immigration Processing Center, about 73 miles south of San Antonio, migrants have complained about the lack of healthy food and medical care, and unsanitary conditions.

Advocates filed a legal motion last month demanding better conditions at Camp East Montana, the nation’s largest immigration detention center, which is inside the Fort Bliss military base in El Paso.

A center in Laredo came under scrutiny this month after the death of a Mexican man, who relatives said was a legal U.S. resident. His daughter said he had not received medicine for a heart condition, diabetes and high blood pressure. An ICE official denied that.

Democrats taking over Congress in January intend to oversee ICE and other immigration agencies closely, using money as a primary lever. Spending bills could be written to withhold or pull back money from agencies that have already received more than $100 billion.

“ICE would be wise to pause the purchases or sales of all of those ICE warehouses,” Mr. Castro said.

The prospect of stopping the San Antonio center is not universally popular. Two council members who lean conservative, Marc Whyte and Misty Spears, disagreed with their colleagues on the question.

“Federal law controls immigration, and City Hall has no business interfering,” they said in a joint statement. “Our residents sent us here to keep them safe, fix our infrastructure and make San Antonio a better place to live. Washington sets immigration policy. We’ve got more than enough work to do right here at home.”

But resistance is growing. A march last month organized by a county commissioner, Tommy Calvert, drew hundreds.

“The facility is woefully inadequate for human beings,” Mr. Calvert said.

Father Drennan said that many of his parishioners feared that they might end up locked inside the 639,595-square-foot warehouse.

“They are trying to make San Antonio the epicenter of the immigration movement, and it’s creating a great sense of fear and anger within the people of our community,” Father Drennan said of the federal government.

item.title: How the Legacy of Torture Has Vexed the Quest for 9/11 Justice
item.description:
The Sept. 11, 2001, terrorist attacks left the World Trade Center in ruins, thousands dead and a stunned nation fearful of what might come next.

In a series of secret actions, the administration of George W. Bush charted a new course to try to prevent more attacks. Dozens of suspected terrorists were spirited off to secret sites for years. Many were tortured by C.I.A. interrogators. No lawyers. No right to remain silent. No Geneva Conventions.

Khalid Shaikh Mohammed, who would later be accused of devising the plot, was stripped naked, rectally abused and waterboarded 183 times. A psychologist threatened to kill his son if more children died in attacks by Al Qaeda.

The agency kept its captives in solitary confinement as it questioned them hundreds of times, effectively training them to believe that if they did not talk, they would be tortured more.

Now, 25 years later, the costs and trade-offs made then are still reverberating in the agonizing wait for a trial in a faraway military court where the legacy of torture hangs over the Sept. 11 case.

Military judges have now thrown out all of the key confessions in the death penalty cases at Guantánamo Bay because the defendants were tortured by the C.I.A.

The fifth and final ruling came early last month. Within weeks, the Supreme Court declined to review a plea deal between prosecutors and Mr. Mohammed and two others accused of conspiracy in the case. The prisoners would have received life sentences in exchange for publicly admitting to their specific roles in the plot.

.

Could this be a turning point for the Sept. 11 families who have waited so long for a day of reckoning? The judge recently set a June 5, 2028, trial date.

“I do think it’s an important moment,” said Jessica Trant, whose father, Dan, a bond trader, was killed at the World Trade Center. “A trial would at least give us the chance to hear the evidence, confront what happened and maybe take back a little of the power we’ve lost along the way.”

That said, Ms. Trant added: “I also know that just because we’re moving toward a trial doesn’t mean we’ll actually get one.”

John Ryan, a former task force commander at ground zero and chief of the Port Authority Police, said two years was too long to wait. He worries that lawyers who have been serving on the case as capital defenders could age out, or another issue could emerge.

“Let’s move the trial date up so that no unforeseen issues can surface,” he said. “This would also support the elder family members who want to see justice in their lifetimes.”

But the other death penalty case at Guantánamo is going first: Jury selection began last month in the trial of a Saudi man who is accused of having a key role in the suicide bombing of a U.S. Navy warship in a harbor in Yemen on Oct. 12, 2000. Seventeen U.S. sailors were killed in the Qaeda attack, and dozens more were wounded.

Hearings in that case recently focused on whether the defendant, Abd al-Rahim al-Nashiri, is too damaged by his torture while he was in C.I.A. custody from 2002 to 2006 to go to trial.

Here is a look at five fateful decisions that led to this day.

Mr. Mohammed was captured in Pakistan in March 2003 and taken to a secret C.I.A. prison in Poland, called a black site. He was, among other things, waterboarded in a desperate search for the whereabouts of Osama bin Laden and information about other potential sleeper cells and plots.

Call it the original sin. The United States could have transferred him to Guantánamo, where the military was holding about 650 detainees from more than 40 countries at the time.

Or, he could have been sent to the United States.

“From the very beginning he said, ‘Take me to New York, give me a lawyer and I’ll be happy to talk to you,’” Rita Radostitz, one of his lawyers, said in court in September 2021. “But instead of doing that, instead of taking him up on that offer, the government made a choice to take a different path.”

But the C.I.A. cannot operate on U.S. soil.

The United States took him on a three-and-a-half-year odyssey through U.S.-controlled prisons from Eastern Europe to Afghanistan, where he was held incommunicado and, according to his lawyer, questioned hundreds of times, sometimes three times a day.

By 2006 the existence of the once-secret prison system had been revealed, and Mr. Bush had the defendants transferred to Guantánamo for trial.

But there was a problem. What the prisoners had told U.S. interrogators hundreds of times in the black sites was undeniably coerced and would be inadmissible at any U.S. court.

Putting them on trial, Bush administration lawyers decided, would require new evidence. So federal agents called “clean teams” were summoned to Guantánamo to obtain fresh confessions.

This time, in January 2007, the prisoners were told their participation was voluntary.

The prisoners were taken in blindfolds and shackles to a former C.I.A. black site at Guantánamo for questioning. The Bush administration also chose to omit a few key components: The prisoners still had not been allowed to consult lawyers, and they were not told that their hundreds of previous statements could not be used against them.

These decisions would prove catastrophic two decades later.

Hearings in the case of Mr. Mohammed and four other men also accused of conspiracy had barely begun when Barack Obama was elected in 2008. The new president suspended the proceedings at Guantánamo.

Attorney General Eric H. Holder Jr. announced, after a period of analysis, that the Obama administration had chosen to put the Sept. 11 defendants on trial in federal civilian court in New York.

The Obama administration did not immediately transfer the defendants to New York or any other trial venue, even as civilian prosecutors concluded they could not use the so-called clean-team confessions.

The federal prosecutors thought they would be inadmissible because the agents who questioned the men at Guantánamo had not read them a Miranda warning.

The decision to try the men in New York had led to a political outcry, and Congress forbade the use of federal funds to transfer them to the United States for trial.

The case was returned to Guantánamo, and military prosecutors chose a different path. They would seek to use the clean-team confessions — which have now been rejected by three military judges and a military court of appeals because of the prisoners’ years of torture and isolation.

Still bitter in 2024, Mr. Holder blamed “the politicians and hacks who second-guessed my decision to bring cases in the effective federal courts.” He said, “Had it not been for their political machinations, Khalid Shaikh Mohammed would just be a bad memory now.”

In 2018 the first military judge in the case, Col. James L. Pohl of the Army, suppressed the clean-team confessions of the then-five defendants in the Sept. 11 case. (Since then, one was found to be mentally unfit to face trial.)The judge ruled that a framework set up by prosecutors to protect C.I.A. secrets was unfair. The information provided to the defense lawyers, the judge ruled, denied them the “particularity and nuance necessary to present a rich and vivid account of the 3-to-4-year period in C.I.A. custody.”

Prosecutors appealed, declaring the 2007 statements crucial capital trial evidence. Years of litigation examined the C.I.A. program of violence and isolation, culminating last month with the military judge throwing out the statements of the fourth and final Sept. 11 defendant.

In the summer of 2024, Defense Secretary Lloyd J. Austin III withdrew from plea agreements that prosecutors had said were “the best path to finality and justice in this case.”

Prosecutors had not so secretly negotiated for years with Mr. Mohammed and two other defendants. In exchange for life sentences, the defendants would openly admit to their specific roles in the hijacking plot that killed 2,976 people and give up nearly every avenue of post-conviction appeal.

Prosecutors would present their case to a military jury. The prisoners agreed to answer written questions from relatives of the dead through a process known as restorative justice.

But Mr. Austin said he was unaware of the deal and chose to revoke it.

That decision led to two more years of litigation. Lower courts ruled that Mr. Austin acted too late to withdraw from the contract; then a civilian court ruled that he had the power to do it. On Oct. 19, the Supreme Court decided not to second-guess Mr. Austin’s authority to make that decision.

For now, the trial of Mr. Mohammed and the others is on track to start on June 5, 2028. Tom Resta has gone to Guantánamo four times to watch the proceedings and has no faith that the trial date will hold.

“We were supposed to have a trial starting in 2021,” said Mr. Resta, whose brother John and sister-in-law Sylvia were killed at the World Trade Center. She was seven months pregnant.
